intro: Drafting a demand letter from scratch is slower than it looks. The blank page makes you decide the facts, the tone, the demand and the structure all at once. The faster route is to start from a vetted precedent, outline the demand, then draft in Word on your Mac. This page covers what the blank page costs, why it happens, fixes you can use for free, and where Lazur helps.
tldr: Starting from a blank page usually costs more time than starting from a vetted precedent.
No source I checked times demand-letter drafting, so time your own drafts for a few weeks.
Outline the parties, facts, demand, deadline and consequence before you write any letter text.
Build one bracketed template in Word and reuse it for the next demand.
Lazur can point, explain and dictate in Word. It does not write or send the letter for you.

blocks.text: A blank page feels like freedom. For a demand letter, it mostly feels like delay. Before you type a sentence you need the parties, the facts in order, the legal basis you rely on, the amount or action you want, a deadline, and the tone your client expects. Miss one of those and the draft stalls halfway through.
What a blank page costs you

The clearest number is your time. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics puts median lawyer pay at $159,670 a year, or $76.76 an hour, based on May 2025 data. That is a salary figure, not a billing rate. Still, it gives you a floor. Every hour spent staring at an empty document is an hour of expensive thinking. Some of that time gets billed and some does not, depending on your client and fee arrangement.

A legal-education vendor, CEB, makes the same point from the practice side. Its guidance says that starting from a blank page 'may seem appealing, but it is often inefficient.' It recommends starting from vetted precedent and working out what the document must do before you draft. That means the blank page is a habit you can change.

Here is the honest gap. No source I checked times how long demand-letter drafting takes. Vendor blogs give time-saving percentages, but those figures were not verified, so this page leaves them out. The only reliable number is the one you measure in your own practice. Treat any unsourced figure as a guess.
How to time your own drafts for a few weeks

Open Apple Notes and start a new note with File > New Note (⌘N). Each time you draft a demand, log the matter type, the date, when you started the outline, when you had a first draft, and when the letter was ready to send. Add one line for each review round.

items: Matter type and jurisdiction, so you compare like with like.
Minutes spent on the outline before you open the draft.
Minutes spent on the first draft, including any copying from precedent.
Minutes on fact checking against the file, the step people skip most often.
Number of review rounds and what changed in each one.

blocks.text: After a few weeks, you will see where the time goes. For most people, the outline and the fact check are the steps that either save time or get dropped. Do not drop either one to look faster on paper.
A worked example: from an unpaid invoice to a sendable letter

Say a client has an unpaid invoice. The invoice is past due, the other side has ignored two emails, and your client wants a letter that sets a deadline and states the next step. Here is the path from blank page to sendable draft.

items: Write the facts list first. Use dates from the invoice, the emails and the engagement letter. Copy amounts exactly as they appear in the file.
Write the demand in one sentence. For example: payment of the amount due by a set date, or the action you will take next.
Pull one precedent from a closed matter with a similar demand. Copy the structure, not the names or numbers.
Replace each fact with a bracketed placeholder first, then fill them from the file one at a time.
Check each legal statement against the source you rely on. Do not trust the precedent's citations without reading them.
Send the draft to a reviewer with the fact list attached, so they check facts before they read the prose.

blocks.text: That last step matters most. A demand letter is mostly facts and claims. Each sentence that states a fact needs a document behind it. Drafting from memory or from an old letter is where dates, names and amounts go wrong. A wrong date can cost you credibility with the other side.
Mistakes that make a blank-page draft worse

items: Writing the opening line first. Write the demand and the deadline first, then the story that supports them.
Writing the legal theory before the timeline is in order. Theory reads well but checks badly against the file.
Starting in a fresh untitled file. Formatting drifts, and the next letter looks different.
Copying a precedent without changing the jurisdiction, the parties or the dates. Old names survive in new letters.
Sending the first draft because it reads well. Good prose can hide a wrong fact.
Pasting client details into a public AI chat window without checking your firm's rules first.

blocks.text: The last mistake deserves more room. Many firms limit which tools can see client information, and some limit AI entirely. Follow your employer's rules on client data before you paste, dictate or screenshot anything. That applies to Lazur, Word with Copilot, and any other tool.
Where AI helps a first draft, and where it does not

The evidence is mixed. The ABA's 2024 survey found AI use among private-practice attorneys rose to 30% from 11%. A 2026 randomized trial by Schwarcz and colleagues gave law students a legal AI tool, a general model, or no AI across six tasks. The abstract reports productivity gains of 50% to 130% in five of six tasks. It also says the tools perform well on drafting persuasive letters.

Those participants were law students, not practicing lawyers. The numbers do not transfer to your desk directly. One summary of the trial gives a different range, so read the paper before you quote it. The same pattern shows up in consulting. A BCG and Harvard study of 758 consultants using GPT-4 found 25% faster work and 40% higher quality on tasks inside the tool's capability, as reported by VentureBeat.

The same study found a warning. People who used AI on tasks outside its capability made more mistakes, because they trusted it when they should not have. Demand letters have plenty of tasks like that, such as interest calculations and local procedural rules.

Legal research tools need caution too. A study by Magesh and colleagues on arXiv found that three legal research tools hallucinated between 17% and 33% of the time. That study covers research tools, not drafting tools, so it does not give a demand-letter error rate. It does tell you to verify every case you cite.

A sensible rule is this. Let the tool produce structure and a rough first pass. You verify every fact, date, citation and legal statement against your own file and sources. If you cannot check a sentence, cut it.
Set up a Word template for demand letters on Mac

Build one template and reuse it. Start with File > New Blank Document (⌘N) in Word. Add your letterhead, the addressee block, a reference line and bracketed placeholders such as [CLIENT NAME], [INVOICE DATE], [AMOUNT DUE] and [RESPONSE DEADLINE]. Placeholders make empty spots easy to see.

items: Set body text and headings once with Home > Styles, so every letter uses the same fonts and spacing.
Add the paragraphs in order: facts, demand, deadline, consequence, and a reservation of rights if your firm uses one.
Add a bracketed note at the top that says to delete it before sending. Reviewers see it first.
Save with File > Save As (⇧⌘S). In the File Format list, choose Word Template (.dotx).
Store the template in a shared folder, and put the year in the file name so old versions are easy to spot.

blocks.text: When a partner edits the draft, turn on Track Changes from the Review tab or with ⌘⇧E. Track Changes keeps each edit visible, so you can see what moved and who moved it. Your firm may have its own rules for returning edited letters to a client file, so follow those.

Word also offers Draft with Copilot. Microsoft's support page describes the flow. You open a blank document, describe the content, submit, then keep, discard, regenerate or refine the result. The feature requires an eligible Microsoft 365 subscription or Microsoft 365 Copilot license. The page does not clearly say which platforms get each drafting feature, so check your Mac version and license first.

blocks.title: A precedent is a starting point
blocks.text: An old demand letter carries old facts, old names and old deadlines. Copy the structure, then rebuild the content from the current file.
Where to find a starting point without a form bank

Not every firm has a document bank, but you can still find precedent. Search your sent mail with the search box at the top of Outlook. Look at letters you sent on closed matters. Ask a colleague which letter they used last time. If your firm allows it, Finder search (⌘F) can help on a shared drive.

CEB's advice is to start from vetted precedent and work out the document's purpose first. The word vetted matters. A letter someone sent last year may have been weak and still got a reply. Ask a senior colleague which precedent they would trust today.
Where Lazur fits into this workflow

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that lives in the notch. Hold ⌥⌘ to ask about anything on screen. Lazur sees your screen, points at things, and answers out loud. It helps with finding things, explaining screens, and getting text into a document by voice.

Hold fn to dictate clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app. That helps with the fact list. Speak the timeline while you read the file, then edit the text in Word. Dictation does not check your facts. You still do that part.

Snippets, a personal dictionary and clipboard slots help with repeated material. Save a standard reservation of rights paragraph as a snippet, if your firm uses one. Use clipboard slots to hold the amount, the invoice date and the deadline while you move between Word and your case file.

Here is what Lazur does not do. It does not write the letter in Word for you, click buttons, edit files or send email. Ask where a button is, and Lazur circles it. Ask how to do a step, and Lazur guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click.

Research works differently. Lazur runs research in its own Chrome tabs through the Lazur for Chrome extension, then returns a summary and a report. Use that to gather public sources on a rule or a case. Then read the primary text yourself before you rely on any of it.
Edge cases that need extra care

Some demand letters break the template. Multiple defendants need one section per party, with the facts for each. Insurance demands often follow a carrier's rules on what the letter must include. Time-sensitive claims need a deadline check against the rules in your jurisdiction. That check belongs to you, not to a tool.

Be careful with interest, fees and penalty figures. Calculate them from the contract and the file, show the arithmetic in the fact table, and have a second person check it. A tool can explain a formula. It should not be the only check on a number that goes out under your name.

Tone is an edge case too. A letter to a repeat client may need a softer opening than a letter to a party who has stopped answering. Decide that with your client before you draft. A blank page does not tell you what the client wants.
What to do next

Start small. This week, time one draft with the log. Next, build one template with placeholders and save it as a Word template. Then pick the precedent you trust most and rewrite its facts from your current file. Keep the outline step even when you are in a hurry.

Before you use any AI tool on a live matter, ask your firm whether it is allowed and what it may see. Only 41% of legal organizations had an AI policy in April 2025, according to Thomson Reuters. If your firm is in the other group, raise the question with the people who set the rules.

faq.question: Can I draft a demand letter from scratch in Word on Mac?
faq.answer: Yes. Start with File > New Blank Document (⌘N) and build the letter from an outline. Microsoft's Draft with Copilot feature needs an eligible Microsoft 365 Copilot license, so check your access before you plan around it.

faq.question: How long does a demand letter take to draft?
faq.answer: No source I checked measures demand-letter drafting time, so no reliable figure exists yet. Time your own drafts for a few weeks in Apple Notes. Your own log will tell you more than a vendor's claim.

faq.question: Is it safe to paste client details into an AI tool?
faq.answer: That depends on your firm's rules, not only on the tool. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer and are not stored. Follow your employer's rules on client data before you use any tool.

faq.question: Does Lazur write the demand letter for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur guides, points, explains and answers out loud. When you dictate, it types text at the cursor. It does not click buttons, edit files or operate other apps for you. You write and check the letter.

faq.question: Can I trust AI-drafted legal text?
faq.answer: Verify all of it. A study by Magesh and colleagues found legal research tools hallucinated between 17% and 33% of the time. That study covers research tools, not drafting tools, but the lesson holds. Check every fact, date and citation against its source.

faq.question: Should I start from a precedent or a blank page?
faq.answer: Start from a vetted precedent. CEB's guidance says a blank page is often inefficient, and recommends working out the document's purpose first. Use your outline to decide what the new letter must do.

problem: drafting demand letters from a blank page

costs.title: Hours you do not get back
costs.text: Drafting time is often the part of a matter nobody tracks. At the BLS median of $76.76 an hour, each hour on a blank page is worth about $77 in salary-equivalent time. That is a rough measure, not a billing rate, but it shows why a fast outline is worth doing.

costs.title: Letters that look different every time
costs.text: When every lawyer starts from a blank page, every letter has its own structure. Reviewers spend time learning each draft before they can check it. A shared template and a shared outline make review faster for everyone.

costs.title: Errors in facts and dates
costs.text: A demand letter with a wrong date or amount can hand the other side an easy reply. Blank-page drafts tend to rely on memory and on whichever file you open first. Check each fact against the document it came from.

costs.title: Extra review rounds
costs.text: A weak first draft moves through more partner rounds. Each round adds days to a matter that may already be waiting on a client decision. Count the rounds in your log to see whether the outline step is working.

costs.title: Stress on a heavy workload
costs.text: Bloomberg Law's Q4 2021 survey of 614 attorneys found burnout 52% of the time. A blank draft adds to a heavy load. No source I checked measures drafting as a cause, so treat this as context, not a diagnosis.

causes.title: Law school taught analysis, not drafting
causes.text: Most law schools teach legal analysis. Practice teaches legal drafting, according to CEB, a legal-education vendor. Legal writing courses focus on memos, briefs and occasional client letters. If you learned demand letters on the job, each new one can feel like a new problem.

causes.title: The facts are spread across the file
causes.text: A demand letter needs dates, amounts and names from emails, invoices, notes and a signed engagement. None of those sit in one place. Before you can write, you have to assemble the facts, and that assembly is the step most people skip.

causes.title: You decide tone, demand and structure at once
causes.text: A blank page asks you to answer every question in one sitting. What do you want, by when, and what happens if the other side ignores you? Until those answers are fixed, every sentence gets rewritten.

causes.title: Perfectionism on the opening paragraph
causes.text: Many drafters stall on the first sentence and rewrite it until the rest of the letter never gets written. A demand letter opening is short. The demand and the deadline matter more than a polished first line.

causes.title: Precedent exists, but you cannot find it
causes.text: Your best letter may sit in an old matter folder or a sent email. Searching takes time, so people start over instead. Starting over feels faster than searching. Usually it is not, and CEB's advice points the same way.

causes.title: The default Word file offers no structure
causes.text: A new blank document in Word gives you an empty page and default styles. There are no placeholders, no reminder to check facts, and no reservation of rights paragraph. Each draft starts from zero because nothing was saved for the next one.

fixes.title: Write the outline before the letter
fixes.text: Use five short lines: parties, facts in date order, the demand, the deadline, and the consequence. Write them in Apple Notes or on paper. Only when all five lines are filled in do you open Word. This takes little time and removes most of the blank-page stall.

fixes.title: Start from one precedent you trust
fixes.text: Find one letter from a closed matter that you or a senior colleague trust. Save a copy under a new name, delete the names, numbers and dates, and keep the structure. Replace each deleted item from the current file, one at a time.

fixes.title: Save a bracketed template once
fixes.text: Use the steps in the Word section above. Bracketed placeholders make empty spots hard to miss. Save the file as a Word template so you never overwrite the master by accident.

fixes.title: Dictate the first pass
fixes.text: Hold fn in Word and speak the paragraphs in order, then edit the text. Speaking can help because you answer a question out loud instead of polishing a sentence. Expect to rewrite the spoken text afterward.

fixes.title: Run a fact check against the file
fixes.text: Make a three-column table in Word: sentence, source document, and the date you checked it. Every fact gets a row. If a fact has no row, it does not go in the letter. Keep this step even when the deadline is close.

fixes.title: Time-box the first draft
fixes.text: Give the first draft a fixed timer and stop when it goes off. A rough draft you can edit beats a polished opening you never finish. Use the Clock timer on your Mac, then write down what is still missing.

fixes.title: Have a reviewer check the facts first
fixes.text: Send the fact table with the draft. Ask the reviewer to check facts before reading the prose. Prose review catches style. Fact review catches the errors that do the most damage in a demand letter.

fixes.title: Verify every citation at the source
fixes.text: If the draft cites a statute or case, open the primary source and read the passage you rely on. The Magesh et al. study found legal research tools hallucinated between 17% and 33% of the time, so do not skip this.

fixes.title: Check your firm's AI and client-data rules
fixes.text: Before you use any AI tool on a live matter, ask your firm what it may see. Only 41% of legal organizations had AI policies in April 2025, according to Thomson Reuters. If the answer is unclear, ask before you paste anything.

fixes.title: Track the time for a month
fixes.text: Use the log from the timing section. After a month, compare outline time, review rounds and fact corrections against the month before. Keep the steps that help and drop the ones that do not.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Time one draft
plan.text: Open Apple Notes and start the timing log. Record the matter type, the start time and the outline time. Do not change how you work yet. You want a baseline before you try anything new.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Write five outline lines
plan.text: For one live or recent matter, write the parties, the facts in date order, the demand, the deadline and the consequence. Stop there. Do not open the letter until all five lines are complete.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Build the template
plan.text: In Word, start with File > New Blank Document. Add letterhead, the addressee block, a reference line and bracketed placeholders. Save it with File > Save As as a Word Template (.dotx) in your firm's shared folder.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Pull one precedent
plan.text: Find one trusted letter from a closed matter. Save a copy, remove names, numbers and dates, and keep the structure. Ask a senior colleague whether they would still use it.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Draft and dictate
plan.text: Use the template. Hold fn in Word and speak the paragraphs in order, then edit. Stop when the timer goes off, even if the letter is not finished. Note how many minutes the draft took.

plan.label: Day 6
plan.title: Build the fact table
plan.text: Create a three-column table in Word with sentence, source and date checked. Every fact gets a row. Remove any sentence that has no source. Send the table with the draft to your reviewer.

plan.label: Day 7
plan.title: Compare and decide
plan.text: Compare your log with the week before. Look at outline time, review rounds and fact corrections. Keep the steps that helped and drop the rest. Follow your firm's rules for any tool you keep.
